paragraphs.en: The interview took place in a disused fish warehouse, which should have warned me.
The founder was an [[immigrant]] [[entrepreneur]] and something of an [[innovator]]; he had spent ten years in shipping before he [[propose]]d a plant that would make [[protein]] for a [[vaccine]].
I was [[eager]] to join, even though the building was cold, damp and deeply [[unattractive]].
He said the plan was [[straightforward]]: turn an empty shell into a clean, [[efficient]] facility by spring.
I liked that he was [[straight]] with me about the money, because the company was almost [[illiquid]].
My first task was a survey of the [[conversion]] itself.
The roof leaked, the [[insulation]] was gone, the walls had to be [[insulated|insulate]] twice over, and the old [[ventilation]] shafts carried more snow than air.
We would need new [[heating]], an [[electric]] boiler and a [[battery]] big enough to carry the freezers through a storm.
The quotes were [[immense]], the price of copper had begun to [[soar]], and the [[technology]] was newer than anything in the town.
The founder wanted to [[recoup]] the money in four years, which struck me as [[prudent]] only if nothing went wrong.
Before we could [[install]] anything, the state regulator sent a [[consultant]] to [[verify]] our plans.
He was [[impartial]] and rather [[bureaucratic]], and he asked for a [[valid]], [[unbiased]] [[account]] of every process.
A [[panel]] of three would [[judge]] the application, and [[disclosure]] of all suppliers was mandatory.
We had to [[subscribe]] to a national register and [[correspond]] with it monthly, which nobody had mentioned.
He warned us that a [[vague]] answer would be read as a [[deceptive]] one.
The neighbours in the [[residential]] street behind us were less enthusiastic.
For them the plant was an [[unwanted]] [[intrusion]], and a few [[oppose]]d it openly at the first public meeting.
One woman [[accuse]]d us of [[invading|invade]] a [[habitat]] that belonged to birds, children and old people.
They saw themselves as the [[victim]]s of a decision made in another city, and a man [[scold]]ed me for ten minutes without once [[glancing|glance]] at the plans.
A single [[instance]] of rudeness can set the tone for a year, and some of their fears were [[undesirable]] for us yet entirely reasonable.
The second meeting turned nasty.
Our opponents used a [[familiar]] [[tactic]]: a series of small [[provocation]]s until someone lost his [[temper]].
The chair, a woman of steady [[temperament]], [[handled|handle]]d it better than I did.
She refused to answer [[random]] questions and insisted on one subject at a time.
I learned that [[tactics]] matter more than volume, and that [[panic]] is often a decision.
By the end of that summer the project had become a legal [[contest]] rather than a technical one.
Our opponents made a [[lame]] argument about property values, and the [[judge]] gave it little weight.
The real [[obstacle]] was not the law but the [[strain]] on the town's narrow roads.
[[Contrary]] to what the local paper printed, we won, though by a narrow [[margin]].
The [[bargain]] we struck was simple: we would pay for the road repairs ourselves.
My roommate is a [[neuroscientist]] who studies [[stress]] and the [[immune]] system.
She says the [[psychology]] of a town under pressure is no [[illusion]]: people [[absorb]] the mood of their neighbours.
A [[gene]] may set a threshold, but the environment decides when it is crossed.
Her favourite [[paradox]] is that the more we [[obsess]] over risk, the worse we [[judge]] it.
I told her about the meeting, and she said a crowd is not stupid, only tired.
At work I began to [[automate]] the sample line, wearing the same white [[garment]] as the operators.
One [[machine]] could do the work of three technicians, and its [[capacity]] doubled our output.
We had to [[obtain]] clean data before we could [[identify]] the [[target]] protein.
Every batch [[varied|vary]] slightly, which made [[accurate]] measurement the whole game.
By March we could [[accomplish]] in a day what had taken a week, and I began to [[deploy]] the spare staff on quality checks.
In April an investor flew in from the capital, a man of [[immense]] energy and [[vast]] ambitions.
He was [[eligible]] for a [[substantial]] tax break, and he wanted a [[bonus]] if we met the deadline.
He asked for a [[version]] of the plan he could show his board, so we [[designate]]d one page as the summary.
I spent a weekend building a [[catalog]] of equipment, and he barely looked at it.
His [[purpose]] was obvious: he wanted a story he could sell, not a plant he could run.
In May a storm came off the sea and took half the roof with it.
Water ran down the new [[insulation]], and the freezers switched to the [[battery]] just in time.
The lane to the plant [[vanished|vanish]]ed under water, and for two days we worked by torchlight.
The [[strain]] on everyone was [[obvious]], and the repairs were [[gradual]] and expensive.
That week taught me to [[abide]] by the weather forecast as much as by the protocol.
In June we invited the neighbours in for an open day.
The hall could [[accommodate]] sixty people, and forty came.
I spoke on [[behalf]] of the company and asked them to [[participate]] in a monitoring group.
It took an hour to [[convince]] the angriest man that we would not [[neglect]] the street.
A [[rebellious]] teenager asked the best question of the afternoon, and the room [[cooperate]]d in a way it never had before.
By the end one woman said she could [[forgive]] the noise, though not the trucks.
The inspection in July was almost pleasant.
The regulator's [[counterpart]] in the health ministry sent a young engineer who [[seldom]] spoke.
She asked about the colour-coded [[stripe]]s on every pipe and the [[vessel]] that held the culture.
She tested the [[nerve]] of the operator on duty by asking him to explain a failed batch from memory.
Her report was [[accurate]] and [[straightforward]], and it [[elevate]]d our standing with the ministry.
That autumn I began to wonder whether this was the [[pursuit]] I wanted.
The plant was [[subject]] to every fashion in the industry, and each [[transition]] cost us a month.
I had [[autonomy]] on paper, yet my days were full of [[distraction]] and [[odd]] hours.
A friend said such doubts were [[inappropriate]] for someone with my [[academic]] record.
In [[contrast]] to him, I thought the doubts were not [[transient]], and that they deserved the [[utmost]] attention.
The founder had left a country where the [[regime]] could change overnight.
He had learned to [[navigate]] customs offices and to keep his [[allegiance]] to nothing but the work.
He said the [[magic]] of a factory is that it makes an idea something you can [[capture]] and share.
People [[elect]] to stay because they can see what they have built.
There was no [[dazzle]] in that, only a slow accumulation of small decisions.
We shipped the first batch in September.
It was not the [[ideal]] outcome: two of the five targets failed, and the [[range]] of tests we could run was still narrow.
The [[general]] conclusion was that the plant would survive, though not in the shape we had imagined.
The founder's answer was [[facile]] and also true: we had [[protect]]ed the thing we set out to build.
It did not [[satisfy]] the neighbours, but it [[occurred|occur]] to me that nobody had ever asked them to help.
